The beam swept across the water at midnight, a slow white finger tracing the same arc it had traced for forty-three years. Elias didn't count the rotations anymore. He counted the things that mattered: the three-gallon oil cans in the cellar (twelve), the days since the supply tender made harbor (seventeen), the letters from his daughter stacked in the desk drawer (two, both unopened).

The light itself was a Fresnel lens, third-order, installed in 1887. Eight hundred pounds of hand-ground prisms floating in a mercury bath. When the mechanism was clean and the weight wound, it turned with a sound like breathing. Tonight it groaned. The mercury had developed a tremor — not enough to stop the rotation, enough to scatter the beam at the edges. Elias had written the Lighthouse Board three times. Three
